2.1.2

(a) Select a subset G of F with the minimal cardinality such that ⋃J∈G​J=⋃I∈F​I. Assume that ⋃J∈G​J is connected, otherwise consider every connected component.
Write G={(ai​,bi​)∣1≤i≤n}. Let G1​={(ai​,bi​)∣i is odd}. We claim that G1​ is a family of mutually disjoint intervals. Otherwise there exists j such that (aj​,bj​)∩(aj+2​,bj+2​)=∅. If bj+1​≤bj+2​, then (aj+1​,bj+1​)⊂(aj​,bj+2​)=(aj​,bj​)∪(aj+2​,bj+2​), so (aj+1​,bj+1​) can be removed; if bj+1​>bj+2​, then (aj+2​,bj+2​)⊂(aj+1​,bj+1​), so (aj+2​,bj+2​) can be removed. In both cases the minimality of G fails.
Similarly we can prove that G2​ is a family of mutually disjoint intervals.
Similar to the proof of Theorem 2.1.6, except for the only difference μ(K)≤μ(Bx​∈F⋃​Bx​)≤μ(Bx​∈G1​⋃​Bx​)+μ(Bx​∈G2​⋃​Bx​)≤α2​∫Eα​​∣f∣dμ.(b) The first inequality is equivalent to ∫X​(∣f∣−α)(χA​−χ∣f∣>α​)dμ≤0.This inequality holds because the integrand is nonpositive whether ∣f∣>α or ∣f∣≤α.
Set Eα​={Mμ​(f)>α}, the following notation follows from the proof of part (a).
Let F1​=⋃Bx​∈G1​​Bx​∩K,F2​=⋃Bx​∈G2​​Bx​∩K, where K is a compact subset of Eα​. We haveμ(K)+μ(F1​∩F2​)​=μ(F1​)+μ(F2​)≤α1​(∫F1​​∣f∣dμ+∫F2​​∣f∣dμ)=α1​(∫K​∣f∣dμ+∫F1​∩F2​​∣f∣dμ).​Take A=F1​∩F2​ in the first inequality and getα1​∫F1​∩F2​​∣f∣dμ−μ(F1​∩F2​)≤α1​∫{∣f∣>α}}​∣f∣dμ−μ({∣f∣>α}).Add up the two inequalities, we obtainμ({∣f∣>α})+μ(K)≤α1​(∫K​∣f∣dμ+∫{∣f∣>α}​∣f∣dμ).Take the supremum in K, and then the required conclusion follows.
When α=1 and f(x)=∣x∣−p1​, M(f)(x)=a−p1​, where a is the positive root of−p1​a1−p1​+∣x∣((1−p1​)a−p1​−∣x∣−p1​)=0.{M(f)(x)>1}={−p1​+∣x∣((1−p1​)−∣x∣−p1​)<0}≜(−A,A).So we have∫{M(f)(x)>1}​(∣f∣−1)=p−1p​A1−p1​−A=−p−12​=−∫{∣f∣>1}​(∣f∣−1).(c) Multiplying the last inequality of part (b) by pαp−1, and integrating with respect to α from 0 to ∞ yields∥f∥Lpp​+∥M(f)∥Lpp​​≤p−1p​(∫R​M(f)p−1∣f∣dμ+∥f∥Lpp​)≤p−1p​(∥M(f)∥Lpp−1​∥f∥Lp​+∥f∥Lpp​).​Let t=∥f∥Lp​∥M(f)∥Lp​​, then(p−1)tp−ptp−1−1≤0.So ∥f∥Lp→Lp​≤Ap​.
(d) According to part (b), ∣x∣−p1​M(f)(x)​ is the positive root of(p−1)xp−pxp−1−1,which means M(f)(x)=Ap​.
Consider fε,N​(x):=∣x∣−p1​+εχN​(∣x∣), where χN​=χ[0,N]​.
It is easy to see thatN→∞lim​ε→0lim​∥fε,N​∥Lp​∥M(fε,N​)∥Lp​​≥Ap​.

2.1.3

(a) Obviously, M(f)≤M(f).
For B(z,r) containing x,∣B(z,r)∣1​∫B(z,r)​∣f∣≤∣B(x,2r)∣2n​∫B(x,2r)​∣f∣.Take the supremum to get M(f)≤2nM(f).
For a ball B containing x, CB​ denotes the minimal cube containing B, then∣B∣1​∫B​∣f∣≤∣B∣∣CB​∣​⋅∣CB​∣1​∫CB​​∣f∣=νn​2n​∣CB​∣1​∫CB​​∣f∣.Take the supremum to get M(f)≤νn​2n​Mc​(f).
For a cube C containing x, BC​ denotes the minimal ball containing C, then∣C∣1​∫C​∣f∣≤∣C∣∣BC​∣​⋅∣BC​∣1​∫BC​​∣f∣=2nn2n​νn​​∣BC​∣1​∫BC​​∣f∣.Take the supremum to get Mc​(f)≤2nn2n​νn​​M(f).
Similar process can be applied to obtain the third inequality.
For f∈L1(Rn),αdMc​(f)​(α)≤αdM(f)​(n2n​νn​2nα​)≤2nn2n​νn​​∥M(f)∥L1,∞​.So Mc​(f)∈L1,∞(Rn).

For f∈Lp(Rn),∥Mc​(f)∥Lp​≤2nn2n​νn​​∥M(f)∥Lp​.So Mc​(f)∈Lp(Rn).
Similarly, Mc​ has the same property.

2.1.4

(a) Write f=fχ{∣f∣>α/2}​+fχ{∣f∣≤α/2}​:=f1​+f2​.
Notice that M(f)≤M(f1​)+M(f2​)≤M(f1​)+α/2, so {M(f)>α}⊂{M(f1​)>α/2}.
From Theorem 2.1.6,μ({M(f)>α})≤μ({M(f1​)>α/2})≤α/23n​∫∣f1​∣dy=α/23n​∫{∣f∣>α/2}​∣f∣dy.So αpμ({M(f)>α})=2p⋅3n(α/2)p−1∫{∣f∣>α/2}​∣f∣dy≤2p⋅3n∥f∥Lpp​,​and hence∥M(f)∥Lp,∞​≤2⋅3n/p∥f∥Lp​.(b) Write f=fχ{∣f∣>1/2}​+fχ{∣f∣≤1/2}​:=f1​+f2​.
Taking p=1 in part (a) yields αdM(f1​)​(α)≤2⋅3n∥f1​∥L1​, so∥M(f1​)∥L1(B)​​=∫1∞​dM(f1​)​(α)dα+∫01​dM(f1​)​(α)dα≤∫1∞​α/23n​∫{∣f∣>1/2}​∣f∣dydα+∫01​∣B∣dα=2⋅3n∫B​(∫1max(1,2∣f∣)​αdα​)∣f∣dy+∣B∣=2⋅3n∥flog+(2∣f∣)∥L1(B)​+∣B∣.​Then M(f) is also integrable over B, as M(f)≤M(f1​)+M(f2​)≤M(f1​)+1/2.

(c) From Theorem 2.1.20, there exists a collection of disjoint open cubes Qj​ such that ⋃Qj​⊂{Mc​(f)>α} and ⋃j​Qj​⊃{f>α}, so∫{∣f∣>α}​∣f∣≤∑∫Qj​​∣f∣≤2nα∑∣Qj​∣.From Exercise 2.1.3,∣{M(f)>cn​α}∣≥∣{Mc​(f)>α}∣≥∑∣Qj​∣≥2nα1​∫{∣f∣>α}​∣f∣.(d) Let x′=ρ2∣x∣−2x for some ρ<∣x∣<2ρ. For y∈B(0,ρ), we have∣x−y∣2−∣x′−y∣2≥(∣x∣−∣x′∣)(∣x∣+∣x′∣−2∣y∣)>0.Consequently, for R>∣x∣−ρ, B(x,R)∩B(0,ρ)⊂B(x′,R), and thus∫B(x,R)​∣f∣=∫B(x,R)∩B(0,ρ)​∣f∣≤∫B(x′,R)​∣f∣,which implies that M(f)(x)≤M(f)(ρ2∣x∣−2x).Using polar coordiantes, the determinant of the map x↦ρ2∣x∣−2x is ±(ρ/∣x∣)2n. Thus we have∫B(0,2ρ)​M(f)(x)dx​≤∫B(0,ρ)​M(f)(x)dx+∫B(0,2ρ)\B(0,ρ)​M(f)(ρ2∣x∣−2x)dx=∫B(0,ρ)​M(f)(x)dx+∫B(0,ρ)\B(0,ρ/2)​M(f)(y)(ρ∣y∣​)2ndy≤(4n+1)∫B(0,ρ)​M(f)(x)dx.​From Exercise 2.1.3, we conclude that ∫B(0,2ρ)​M(f)(x)dx≤2n(4n+1)∫B(0,ρ)​M(f)(x)dx.(e) For x∈/2B,M(f)(x)=x∈B,diamB>ρsup​∣B∣1​∫B​∣f∣dx<∣B∣2n​∥f∥L1​=λ0​.Therefore we have∫2B​M(f)(x)dx​≥∫cn−1​λ0​∞​∣{x∈2B∣M(f)(x)>cn​α}∣dα=∫cn−1​λ0​∞​∣{M(f)>cn​α}∣dα≥∫cn−1​λ0​∞​α2−n​∫{∣f∣>α}​∣f(y)∣dydα=2−n∫{∣f∣>α}​(∫cn−1​λ0​max(∣f∣,cn−1​λ0​)​αdα​)∣f(y)∣dy=2−n∥flog+(λ0−1​cn​∣f∣)∥L1​,​where the second inequality is from part (c).
From part (d),∫2B​M(f)(x)dx≤2n(4n+1)∫B​M(f)(x)dx,and then the required conclusion follows.

We have=≤≤=​∫A​∣S(f)∣qdx∫0∞​qαq−1∣A∩{S(f)>α}∣dα∫0∣A∣B​∥f∥L1​​qαq−1∣A∣dα+∫∣A∣B​∥f∥L1​∞​qαq−1αB​∥f∥L1​dα(∣A∣B​∥f∥L1​)q∣A∣+1−qq​(∣A∣B​∥f∥L1​)q−1B∥f∥L1​1−q1​Bq∥f∥L1q​∣A∣1−q.​The second result follows from taking S=M, then B=3n.

2.1.6

(a) Define M1(i)​:=bi​−ai​1​(ai​,bi​)∋xi​sup​∫ai​bi​​∣f(y1​,⋯,yn​)∣dyi​.It is obvious that Ms​(f)(x)=M1(1)​∘⋯∘M1(n)​(f)(x).
Thus, ∫Rn​Ms​(f)(x)pdx​≤∫Rn​M1(1)​∘⋯∘M1(n)​(f)(x)pdx1​⋯dxn​≤App​∫Rn−1​M1(2)​∘⋯∘M1(n)​(f)(x)pdx2​⋯dxn​≤⋯≤Appn​∥f∥Lpp​.​(b) Consider gε,N​(x):=j=1∏n​fε,N​(xj​) where fε,N​(xj​):=∣xj​∣−p1​+εχN​(∣xj​∣).
From Exercise 2.1.2 (c), ∥Ms​∥≥Apn​, so ∥Ms​∥=Apn​.
(c) Consider fm​=mnχ[0,m1​]n​, then ∥f∥L1​=1.
For x∈Em​:={i=1∏n​xi​≤1,xi​≥m1​,i=1,⋯,n}, write Rx​=i=1∏n​[0,xi​], we haveMs​(fm​)(x)≥∣Rx​∣1​∫Rx​​fm​(x)dx=∣Rx​∣1​∥fm​∥L1​≥1.Thus∥fm​∥L1​∥Ms​(fm​)∥L1,∞​​≥∣{Ms​(fm​)≥1}∣≥∣Em​∣.Yet let m→∞, by the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem and Tonelli’s theorem, m→∞lim​∣Em​∣​=∫i=1∏n​xi​≤1,xi​>0,i=1,⋯,n​dx1​⋯dxn​=∫Rn−1​x2​⋯xn​1​dx2​⋯dxn​(∫R​x1​dx)n−1=∞.​So Ms​ is not of weak type (1,1).

2.1.8

Let f0​ be the characteristic function of the unit ball B in Rn. Note thatM(f0​)(x)≥∣Bx​∣1​∫Bx​​f0​(y)dy,where Bx​=B(21​(∣x∣−∣x∣−1)∣x∣x​,21​(∣x∣+∣x∣−1)) for ∣x∣>1.
For z∈B(0,1),z∈Bx​​⇔∣∣​z−21​(∣x∣−∣x∣−1)∣x∣x​∣∣​2<∣∣​21​(∣x∣+∣x∣−1)∣∣​2⇔∣z∣2−(∣x∣−∣x∣−1)∣x∣z⋅x​<∣∣​21​(∣x∣+∣x∣−1)∣∣​2−∣∣​21​(∣x∣−∣x∣−1)∣∣​2⇔(−∣x∣+∣x∣−1)∣x∣z⋅x​<1−∣z∣2⇐z⋅x>0.​This means half of the unit ball {z∈B∣z⋅x>0} is contained in Bx​, implying thatM(f0​)(x)≥∣Bx​∣∣B∣/2​=(21​(∣x∣+∣x∣−1))−n/2.So ∥f0​∥Lpp​∥M(f0​)∥Lpp​​​≥∣B∣1​∫∣x∣>1​[(21​(∣x∣+∣x∣−1))−n/2]pdx=2pn​∫1∞​rn−1(21​(r+r−1))−npdr​Let f(r)=r(21​(r+r−1))−p. Then f(1)=1 and f′(1)=1, so f(r)>1 on some interval (1,r0​). Therefore,∥f0​∥Lpp​∥M(f0​)∥Lpp​​≥2pn​∫1∞​rf(r)n​dr>2pn​∫1r0​​rdr​→∞as n→∞.​

2.1.9

Consider the Besicovitch Set Eε​ (see Elias M. Stein, Harmonic Analysis, X.1, p.435), which satisfies
(1) Eε​ is a union of 2N rectangles R1​,⋯,R2N​, each having side lengths 1 and 2−N, and ∣Eε​∣<ε, and
(2) the Rj​’s are mutually disjoint, j=1,⋯,2N. Here the Rj​ is defined to be the rectangle obtained by translating Rj​ by two units along the longer side of Rj​.
So ∥χEε​​∥Lpp​<ε, and for x∈Rj​, M0​(χEε​​)(x)≥31​, which implies that ∥M0​(χEε​​)∥Lpp​≥31​.Let ε→0, and then we can see the unboundedness.
Notice that M0​ is weak type (∞,∞), if M0​ is weak type (1,1), from the Marcinkiewicz interpolation theorem, M0​ is strong type (2,2). Contradiction!
(b) Lemma: Let {B1​,⋯,Bk​} be a finite collection of open rectangles in R2, whose eccentricity is b. Then there exists a finite subcollection of pairwise disjoint rectangles {Bj1​​,⋯,Bjl​​} such that 16b2r=1∑l​∣Bjr​​∣≥∣i=1⋃k​Bi​∣.Proof of lemma: First notice that if two rectangles with eccentricity b intersect, we claim that the smaller one B is contained in the bigger one A scaled 4b times.
We place the center of A at 0, the longer edge being parallel to the x-axis. Let the length of the edge of A,B be 1,b;c,bc, where c<1.
So the abscissa of points in B is no more than 21​+diamB≤4b⋅21​, and the ordinate of points in B is no more than 2b​+diamB≤4b⋅2b​.
This implies 4bA⊃B.
Then follows the proof of Lemma 2.1.5 to prove the lemma. Similar to the proof of Theorem 2.1.6, we see that ∥M00​(f)∥L1,∞​≤16b2∥f∥L1​.(c) Notice that for rectangles A,B satisfying the assumption above, if A and B intersect, ∣A∣≥∣B∣, then 3A⊂B. The coefficient 3 does not depend on the {a2​,⋯,an​}.
Then we can deduce the similar conclusion as in part (b).

2.1.10

(a) Define Of​(y)=ε→0limsup​∣Tε​(f)(y)∣, then for y∈D,Of​(y)≤K((Of−g​(y)+Og​(y))=KOf−g​(y).

We claim μ{Of​(y)>δ}=0,∀δ>0.

Note that ∀η>0,∃g∈D,∥f−g∥Lp​<η. So we have μ{Of​(y)>δ}​≤μ{Of−g​(y)>δ/K}≤μ{T∗​(f−g)>δ/K}≤(K/δ∥T∗​(f−g)∥Lq,∞​)q≤(K/δ∥T∗​∥Lp→Lq,∞​∥f−g∥Lp​)q.​

Let η→0, we have proved our assertion, which implies that ε→0limsup​∣Tε​(f)(y)∣=0.

(b) DefineTε​(f)(x):=x∈Bsup​(∣B∣1​∫B​∣f(y)−f(x)∣pdy)p1​.By Minkowski’s inequality, we have (∫B​∣f(y)−f(x)+g(y)−g(x)∣pdy)p1​≤(∫B​∣f(y)−f(x)∣pdy)p1​+(∫B​∣g(y)−g(x)∣pdy)p1​.So we have Tε​(f+g)≤Tε​(f)+Tε​(g).
When p≥1, by Minkowski’s inequality, (∫B​∣f(y)−f(x)∣pdy)p1​≤(∫B​∣f(y)∣pdy)p1​+∣f(x)∣≤∣f∣+M(∣f∣p)p1​;when p<1, by part (c) of Exercise 1.1.5, (∫B​∣f(y)−f(x)∣pdy)p1​​≤(∫B​∣f(y)∣p+∣f(x)∣pdy)p1​≤2p1​−1((∫B​∣f(y)∣pdy)p1​+∣f(x)∣)≤2p1​−1(∣f∣+M(∣f∣p))p1​.​Note that M:L1→L1,∞ is bounded, we have δpμ{M(∣f∣p)p1​}=δpμ{M(∣f∣p)>δp}≤∥fp∥L1​⋅∥M∥=∥f∥Lpp​⋅∥M∥.So f↦M(∣f∣p)p1​ is of weak type (p,p), and the norm is less equal to ∥M∥p1​, which implies T∗​ is of weak type (p,p). For f continuous, T∗​(f)=0, and C(Rn) is dense in Lp(Rn). Then we finish the proof by part (a).
(c) Set Q=[0,1]n, then fχQ+m​∈L1(Rn),m∈Zn. Apply part (b) to fχQ+m​, we have f(x)=0, a.e. on every m+Q, therefore a.e. on Rn.

2.1.11

(a) It’s easy to see Eα​:={MR​(f)>α} is open.
Write Eα​=⨄(ai​,bi​). For x∈(aj​,bj​), let Nx​={s∣∫xs​∣f∣dt>α(s−x)}∩(x,bj​].The set Nx​ is nonempty, and supNx​=bn​. Otherwise, there exists r>0 s.t. ∫xx+r​∣f(t)∣dt>αr. Thus x+r>bn​, namely r>bn​−x. But as bn​∈/Eα​, ∫bn​bn​+r′​∣f(t)∣dt≤αr′ for all r′>0. Take r′=x+r−bn​, then ∫bn​x+r​∣f(t)∣dt≤α(x+r−bn​). This leads to ∫xbn​​∣f(t)∣dt>α(bn​−x), whence bn​∈Nx​, contradiction! Let s0​=supNx​, then ∀ϵ>0,∃sϵ​ such that ∫xsϵ​​∣f∣>α(s−x). If s0​<bj​, from the definition of Eα​, there exists s0′​>s0​, such that ∫s0​s0′​​∣f∣>α(s0′​−s0​).
Let ϵ→0,∫xs0′​​∣f∣>α(s0′​−x), contradictory to the supremum. So s0​=bj​.
Let x→aj​,∫aj​bj​​∣f∣≥α(bj​−aj​). If ∫aj​bj​​∣f∣>α(bj​−aj​), then aj​∈Eα​, a contradiction. Thus,∫aj​bj​​∣f∣=α(bj​−aj​),which implies that ∣MR​(f)>α∣=α1​∫{M(f)>α}​∣f∣dt.Similar for ML​(f).

(b)∥MR​(f)∥Lpp​​=∫0∞​pαp−1α1​∫{M(f)>α}​∣f∣dtdα=p−1p​∫Rn​M(f)p−1∣f∣dt≤p−1p​∥MR​(f)∥Lpp−1​∥f∥Lp​.​Here we use Hölder’s inequality for the last inequality. Then we get∥MR​(f)∥Lp​≤p−1p​∥f∥Lp​.(c) Consider fε,N​:=x−p1​+εχ(0,N)​.
We have ∥fε,N​∥Lpp​=∫0N​x−1+εpdx=εp1​Nεp, M(f)(x)=x1​∫0x​t−p1​+εdt=1−p1​+εx−p1​+ε​.So∥M(fε,N​)∥Lpp​≥∫0N​(1−p1​+εx−p1​+ε​)pdx=(1−p1​+ε1​)p⋅εp1​Nεp.Let ε→0, then ∥M∥≥p−1p​.

2.3.6

The Fourier transform of a nonzero C0∞​ function, as a distribution with compact support, is a real analytic function by Theorem 2.3.21, which cannot be a C0∞​ function for it would otherwise be identically 0 due to the uniqueness of real analytic functions (the uniqueness is obtained by showing that the interior of the zero set of a real analytic function is both open and closed).

Assume the converse. Then for all f∈Lp(Rn), f^​ is locally integrable and hence the map f→f^​ is a well defined operator from Lp(Rn) to L1(B(0,M)) for all M>0 (i.e. ∥f^​∥L1(B(0,M))​<∞ for all f∈Lp(Rn), since B(0,M) is covered by a finite number of neighborhoods of x∈B(0,M)​ on which f^​ is integrable).

Then we shall use the closed graph theorem to deduce that the operator is bounded, or in other words, ∥f^​∥L1(B(0,M))​≤CM​∥f∥Lp(Rn)​.

Suppose (fn​,fn​^​)→(f,g) in Lp(Rn)×L1(B(0,M)), then by Proposition 2.3.22, fn​→f in S′, so fn​^​→f^​ in S′. Note that fn​^​→g in L1(B(0,M)) implies convergence in S′, so we can conclude that g is indeed f^​ once we check that: if two L1 functions are identical as tempered distributions, then they are the same as functions.

In fact, if for all φ∈S, ∫Rn​f^​φ=∫Rn​gφ, then so will be true for φ=χ{f^​≥g}​−χ{f^​<g}​, which is justified by finding a sequence of Schwartz functions all bounded by 1 converging pointwise to φ and making use of the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem — such Schwartz functions can be taken as a sequence of step functions χAn​​−χBn​​ mollified at the endpoints approximating φ, where the An​’s and Bn​’s are each a finite combination of intervals contained in {f^​≥g} and {f^​<g} with m({f^​≥g}\An​)→0 and m({f^​<g}\Bn​)→0. Then we get f^​=g in the usual sense of functions.

To violate the previous inequality ∥f^​∥L1(B(0,M))​≤CM​∥f∥Lp(Rn)​ whenever p>2, takefN​(x)=t−ne−πt−2∣x∣2,where t=(1+iN)1/2. Then for Re(t−2)=1+N21​=∣t∣−4,∥fN​∥Lp(Rn)​=∣t∣−n(∫Rn​e−π(∣t∣−2∣x∣)2pdx)p1​=∣t∣(−1+p2​)n∥e−π∣x∣2∥Lp(Rn)​.

AndfN​​(ξ)=(t−nδt−1(e−π∣x∣2))∧(ξ)=(δtf)(ξ)=e−π∣ξ∣2(1+iN)using Proposition 2.2.11 and Example 2.2.9, so ∥fN​​∥L1(B(0,M))​=∥e−π∣ξ∣2∥L1(B(0,M))​ is a constant. Therefore the inequality cannot be true, for ∣t∣(−1+p2​)n→0 as N→∞.
